body.x: The nikah nama looks more frightening than it is. It is a long printed form, often in a language you half-read, produced at the most emotional hour of the wedding day and signed in front of everyone you know. But underneath the formal wording it is a simple document: it records who is marrying whom, what has been agreed, and who witnessed it. This page walks through it the way a kind relative would — in everyday words, section by section — so that when the pen reaches you, you know what your hand is doing.
First, what kind of document is this?

The nikah nama is the written record of the marriage contract — the aqd — that is spoken aloud at the ceremony. The spoken contract is the marriage itself; the paper is its proof and its memory. That is why accuracy matters more than speed: names, dates and figures written here follow the couple into passports, visas, inheritance and, if it ever comes to it, courts. Forms differ between countries and even between officiants, and your own marja's requirements govern the religious side, but the sections below appear in some order on almost every version.
The names at the top: who is marrying whom

The first sections name the bride and groom fully, with their fathers' names, ages and addresses, and they name the wali — the bride's guardian, usually her father — and the wakeel, the representative who speaks the contract's words on each side if the couple do not recite them personally. Read these lines like a proofreader, not a guest. A misspelt name or a wrong date of birth is a small embarrassment today and a genuine bureaucratic problem later, when this document must match identity papers exactly. It is entirely normal to stop and correct the form before anything is signed.
The mahr section: the money paragraph

Next comes the mahr — the gift the groom owes the bride as her own right, not a payment to her family. The form usually splits it into two parts. The prompt portion is due at the time of the nikah or whenever the bride asks for it. The deferred portion is recorded as owed, and becomes payable on the agreed terms — commonly on demand or if the marriage ends. In plain words: whatever figure is written here is the figure that counts, whatever was said in family discussions. Check that the amount, and the split between prompt and deferred, matches what was actually agreed, and that the currency is stated. If it does not match, this is the moment to say so — quietly, to the officiant, before signatures.
The conditions: the pages everyone skips

Most forms leave space for conditions agreed by the couple, and in some countries printed standard conditions appear here too — including, on some forms, a clause about delegated right of divorce. This is the section couples most often sign unread, and it is the one with the longest consequences. A condition written and accepted here is part of the contract, not a footnote. A printed clause that has been struck through has been deliberately removed — ask who removed it and why, and do not accept 'it is standard' as an explanation of a deletion. You do not need to add conditions; many couples add none. But you do need to know whether any are present, and what each one says, in words you understand.
Three things to never sign unread

The mahr figures — the total, the prompt and deferred split, and the currency, exactly as written.
Any struck-through or handwritten change anywhere on the form — every alteration should be explained and initialled.
The conditions section — including the printed clauses about delegated divorce where the form has them — whether you are adding conditions or not.
Each of these takes under a minute to check. The habit to build is simple: the person who signs slowly is not being difficult; they are being married carefully.
Signatures, witnesses and the officiant's seal

At the end, the bride and groom sign — the bride often signing first, sometimes from an adjoining room through her wakeel in traditional settings — followed by the witnesses and the officiant's stamp or signature. The witnesses are not decoration: they are the people who can later testify that this contract happened, between these people, on these terms. Keep the family's copy somewhere it will survive: the nikah nama is requested again and again across a life — for a spouse visa, for registering the marriage civilly where that is a separate step, for children's documents. Photograph it, and keep the original flat and dry.
Questions to ask the officiant before the day

Which form will you use, and may we read a blank copy this week?
How do you record the mahr, and can the prompt and deferred amounts be written exactly as we have agreed?
Are there printed conditions on your form, and will you explain each one to us before the ceremony?
Who will act as wakeel for each side, and what exactly will they say on our behalf?
What do we receive afterwards, and how do we get a certified copy if we need one?

A good officiant welcomes these questions; they are the sign of a couple taking the contract seriously. Ask them days before, not minutes before. Then, when the ceremony comes, you can give the words themselves your full attention — which is what the day is for. Couples who met through family, community or a platform such as Shia Rishta all arrive at the same table and the same form; the ones who read it first sign it with the calmest hands.

title: Shia nikah nama explained: every clause simply
